name: Covenant Extraction
title: Covenant Extraction
answer: Covenant extraction is the work of pulling the specific financial and behavioural promises out of a credit agreement and turning them into structured terms a system can test. It covers maintenance and incurrence covenants, baskets, carve-outs, thresholds, defined terms and the cross-references that tie them together. In fixed income and credit risk the output feeds monitoring, valuation and reporting rather than replacing the analyst's reading of the document. The scope runs from a single clause to a full indenture, and the hard part is usually the definitions, not the headline ratio.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Covenant extraction is the work of pulling the specific financial and behavioural promises out of a credit agreement and turning them into structured terms a system can test. It covers maintenance and incurrence covenants, baskets, carve-outs, thresholds, defined terms and the cross-references that tie them together. In fixed income and credit risk the output feeds monitoring, valuation and reporting rather than replacing the analyst's reading of the document. The scope runs from a single clause to a full indenture, and the hard part is usually the definitions, not the headline ratio.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the loan or bond documents themselves, typically PDFs of credit agreements, indentures and amendments, plus any prior extraction held in a deal database. Processing sits on document parsing and optical character recognition for scanned files, a store for the source text and its page anchors, and a schema or data model that holds each covenant as a structured record. Large language models are commonly used for the reading step, with conventional rules and a database behind them for storage and query. Access control matters because these documents are often confidential and sometimes under distribution restrictions.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical pipeline converts the document to text, splits it into sections and clauses, then classifies passages as covenants, definitions or boilerplate. Extraction pulls the parties, the test, the threshold, the measurement period and the defined terms, and resolves references so a ratio points at the right definition. Because models misread numbers and negations, the output is checked against the source, either by a human reviewer or by a second pass that compares the extracted value with the quoted text. Results are stored with the clause and page they came from so any figure can be traced back.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are a missed covenant, a wrong threshold and a definition applied out of context, any of which can misstate a borrower's position. Every extracted term should carry its source clause and page, the model or rule that produced it, the date and the reviewer, so an audit can reconstruct the decision. Credit agreements are frequently confidential, so handling, retention and access need to match the agreement and any internal policy. Outputs are decision support for credit professionals, not legal advice, and material terms are normally confirmed against the executed document before they are relied on.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Accuracy on definitions, baskets and cross-references is where most effort is going, since these drive the errors that matter. Expect tighter links between extracted covenants and the financial data used to test them, so a breach signal can be raised and evidenced rather than assembled by hand. Amendment tracking is a natural next step, because a covenant set changes over the life of a deal and the current version is the one that counts. Reviewers are likely to shift from reading every clause to checking flagged passages and exceptions, with the audit trail becoming the main product of the work.
